commenti.body:
Surrealism proper is heavily associated with what André Breton called "pure psychic automatism", the most characteristic form of which would be free association basically, automatic writing. But surrealist-affiliated artists like Man Ray, Dali, and Buñuel made use of cinema as a medium. They eschew conventional narrative and characterization, introduce bizarre juxtapositions (what Breton, quoting Isidore Ducasse, might call chance encounters), and techniques meant to bridge somewhat the gap between dreams and everyday life. They were also ardent Marxists who fervently believed that the revolution would create a world in which everybody was a poet. They were staunchly anti-institutional, playful, kind of straddling the line between the theoretical and the irrational, playing with the possibilities which exist at that junction.

The term has been watered down a bit since the manifestos were written. There have been claims that surrealism's been recuperated tout court. Plenty of people are called surrealist whose work doesn't quite measure up to the rather high expectations of Breton. That being said, I would recommend Raul Ruiz, Luis Buñuel, Guy Maddin, Patrick Bokanowski, and Leos Carax as great artists broadly identifiable as surrealist filmmakers.

Surrealism was an early 20th century intellectual/artistic practice that appropriated a Freudian view of the unconscious.  It's practitioners hoped to invigorate the arts by drawing ideas, images, and words from their own unconscious minds (with minimal conscious input) aiming to speak to and effect the unconscious minds of spectators, bypassing the spectator's typical cognitive and sensory categories or intuitions.  If you look up "automatic writing" you'll get a good sense of their creative process. 

The major technique in early 20th century art was *juxtaposition*.  By slamming very different images or objects together in a temporal sequence (in film) or onto the same canvas (in painting) new meanings emerge and create a different, often somewhat uncanny, reaction in the viewer.  The goal was to liberate both art works and people (most surrealists were leftists).

Surrealism in film is tricky to pull off because of the inherent objectivity of the camera (some experimental filmmakers quit using film to represent at all - they might just scratch undeveloped film stock, process it, and randomly edit the sections of film, and then project it).  Surrealist films usually settle for using actual footage of people, places, and things but they use various techniques to render watching their footage more dreamlike (Freud described dreams as 'the royal road to the unconscious').

Perhaps the flaw in all this is that watching a film is a conscious activity and, thus, the structures of human cognition are always at work instantly.  They can, of course be bypassed to some degree by having the spectator in an altered state.  But viewing almost *any* film while on LSD will create a perhaps uncanny or liberating experience, so you don't need to create a surrealist film to provoke a surreal response in such people.

Some already great comments here, but I would add that what separates surrealism from fourth wall breaks is that the fourth wall breaks in something like Amelie are not irrational. The character is interacting with or acknowledging the audience, but is not inherently breaking the logic of the film, because the main character is responding to or talking about what we are all seeing.

For a good example of the irrationality/dream logic of surrealism, see in Buñuel's The Discreet Charm of the Bourgeoisie, where increasingly illogical events happen to interrupt the dinner party, yet no character actually acknowledges what is happening with any kind of "realistic" reaction. It is the juxtaposition of the events of the film to the characters' (non-)reactions to them that creates the surrealism. If the same illogical things happened but the characters responded to them "realistically", I would say that is when the genre becomes more like fantasy, horror or magical realism.

A true surrealist fourth wall break would be for the character to turn to camera and then talk about something completely different, in order to introduce an irrational, subtextual or philosophical commentary, particularly one that is totally juxtaposed to what we what just seen.

A good example of this kind of surrealist fourth wall breaking is something Monty Python often did, more so in their Flying Circus TV series than their film work, where a character would often step out of a sketch to address the audience and change tack from what we've just been watching. Sometimes these interruptions would be in the form of Terry Gilliam's animation, which I would say broadly fit into the genre of surrealism.
